nodes.label: Sets and Relations
nodes.note: Sets, counting and relations form the language JEE uses to state algebra and probability problems. Expect one or two direct questions per shift, usually on Venn counting or on checking an equivalence relation.

nodes.label: Set Fundamentals
nodes.note: How a set is written and which standard number sets exist. Everything later depends on reading a set-builder rule correctly.

nodes.label: Definition and Notation
nodes.note: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, and $a \in A$ states membership while $a \notin A$ denies it. JEE exploits 'well-defined' by offering vague collections such as 'the best cricketers in India'.

nodes.label: Standard Number Sets
nodes.note: The usual chain is $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{W} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}$. Rational numbers are $\mathbb{Q} = \{p/q : p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, \ q \neq 0\}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ covers every complex number.

nodes.label: Roster and Set-Builder Form
nodes.note: Roster form lists the elements, set-builder form gives the defining rule. Always expand the rule into a list before you start counting.

nodes.label: Example: Roster Expansion
nodes.note: The builder $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : |x| \le 3\}$ expands to $\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$, so the cardinality is $n(A) = 7$.

nodes.label: Types of Sets
nodes.note: Classification by size and by comparison. The empty set trap and the equal-versus-equivalent distinction are the two favourites of paper setters.

nodes.label: Empty and Singleton Sets
nodes.note: The empty set satisfies $n(\phi) = 0$, yet $\{\phi\}$ is a singleton with exactly one element. Options built on this confusion appear almost every year.

nodes.label: Finite, Infinite and Cardinality
nodes.note: The cardinality $n(A)$ counts distinct elements of a finite set, and $n(\phi) = 0$. Infinite sets such as $\mathbb{R}$ carry no finite count, so count questions always restrict to a finite universe.

nodes.label: Equal vs Equivalent Sets
nodes.note: Equivalent means $n(A) = n(B)$, while equal means $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$ together, giving $A = B$. Equal sets are always equivalent, but equivalent sets need not be equal.

nodes.label: Subsets and Power Sets
nodes.note: Subset logic and the $2^n$ power-set count drive quick option-based questions where all subsets must be enumerated.

nodes.label: Subset and Proper Subset
nodes.note: $A \subseteq B$ means every element of $A$ lies in $B$, and $A \subset B$ adds $A \neq B$. The empty set is a subset of every set, which makes it the default element of any intersection.

nodes.label: Power Set
nodes.note: $P(A)$ collects all subsets of $A$, so $n(A) = n$ gives $n(P(A)) = 2^n$. The power set is never empty because $\phi \in P(A)$.

nodes.label: Example: Power Set of a Two-Element Set
nodes.note: For $A = \{1, 2\}$ we get $P(A) = \{\phi, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}\}$. Here $A \in P(A)$ is true but $\{A\} \notin P(A)$, a distinction worth memorising.

nodes.label: Disjoint and Comparable Sets
nodes.note: Two sets are disjoint when $A \cap B = \phi$, and comparable when one contains the other. Disjointness is exactly what lets you drop the intersection term in counting formulas.

nodes.label: Real Intervals
nodes.note: Closed and open intervals are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, for example $[a, b] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a \le x \le b\}$. Mixed forms such as $[a, b)$ show up constantly in domain and range answers.

nodes.label: Set Operations and Algebraic Laws
nodes.note: Union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and complement, together with the laws that regroup them. Every De Morgan question reduces to one of these rules.

nodes.label: Union of Sets
nodes.note: $A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$ gathers every element of either set. It is commutative and associative, with identity $A \cup \phi = A$.

nodes.label: Intersection of Sets
nodes.note: $A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$ keeps only common elements, and $A \cap \phi = \phi$. Intersection distributes over union: $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$.

nodes.label: Difference of Sets
nodes.note: $A - B = A \cap B'$ removes from $A$ everything that also lies in $B$. Consequently $A - B = A$ holds exactly when $A \cap B = \phi$.

nodes.label: Symmetric Difference
nodes.note: $A \Delta B = (A - B) \cup (B - A)$ is the exclusive part of the union, and $n(A \Delta B) = n(A) + n(B) - 2n(A \cap B)$. It distributes over intersection: $A \cap (B \Delta C) = (A \cap B) \Delta (A \cap C)$.

nodes.label: Complement and De Morgan Laws
nodes.note: De Morgan gives $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ and $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$, alongside $A \cup A' = U$ and $A \cap A' = \phi$. Flip the operation and swap the sets.

nodes.label: Example: Complement Counting
nodes.note: If $n(U) = 50$ and $n(A \cap B) = 12$, then $n((A \cap B)') = n(U) - n(A \cap B) = 38$. Complement questions are subtraction from the universe and nothing more.

nodes.label: Commutative, Associative and Idempotent Laws
nodes.note: $A \cup B = B \cup A$, $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$ and $A \cup A = A$, with mirror laws for intersection. These let you regroup a long union while shading a Venn diagram.

nodes.label: Cardinality and Counting
nodes.note: Inclusion-exclusion on finite sets. This is where most JEE Main set questions actually live.

nodes.label: Two-Set Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.note: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$, and the intersection term disappears for disjoint sets. This is the most used counting identity in the chapter.

nodes.label: Example: Survey Counting
nodes.note: If 30 students like physics, 25 like chemistry and 10 like both, then $n(P \cup C) = 30 + 25 - 10 = 45$ of the surveyed students like at least one.

nodes.label: Three-Set Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.note: $n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(B \cap C) - n(C \cap A) + n(A \cap B \cap C)$. Add singles, subtract pairs, then add back the triple overlap.

nodes.label: Elements in Exactly Two Sets
nodes.note: $n(A \cap B) + n(B \cap C) + n(C \cap A) - 3n(A \cap B \cap C)$ counts elements lying in precisely two of the three sets. The coefficient 3 strips out the triple overlap counted in every pair.

nodes.label: Elements in Exactly One Set
nodes.note: $n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - 2[n(A \cap B) + n(B \cap C) + n(C \cap A)] + 3n(A \cap B \cap C)$ counts elements in exactly one set. Most-attempted region in a three-circle Venn diagram.

nodes.label: Counting Differences
nodes.note: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$ and $n(B - A) = n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. Use these when only one region is asked, instead of shading the whole diagram.

nodes.label: Cartesian Products
nodes.note: Ordered pairs and product sets. This is the bridge from sets to relations and functions, so it appears in both chapters.

nodes.label: Ordered Pairs
nodes.note: $(a_1, b_1) = (a_2, b_2)$ holds iff $a_1 = a_2$ and $b_1 = b_2$, so order matters and $(1, 2) \neq (2, 1)$. This single idea is why $(a, b) \neq (b, a)$ in counting questions.

nodes.label: Cartesian Product Definition
nodes.note: $A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\}$ and $n(A \times B) = n(A) n(B)$. Also $A \times B = \phi$ exactly when at least one of the sets is empty.

nodes.label: Properties of the Product
nodes.note: $(A \times B) \cap (C \times D) = (A \cap C) \times (B \cap D)$, and $A \subseteq B, C \subseteq D$ implies $A \times C \subseteq B \times D$. Distribution over union, intersection and difference all hold.

nodes.label: Example: Shared Ordered Pairs
nodes.note: If $A$ and $B$ have $n$ elements in common, then $A \times B$ and $B \times A$ share exactly $n^2$ ordered pairs, because both coordinates must be shared.

nodes.label: Relations
nodes.note: A relation is simply a subset of a product set. Domain, range, inverse and composition follow from that reading.

nodes.label: Relation as a Subset
nodes.note: A relation $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is any subset of $A \times B$, written $aRb$ for $(a, b) \in R$. With $n(A) = m$ and $n(B) = n$ there are $2^{mn}$ possible relations.

nodes.label: Domain, Range and Codomain
nodes.note: $\text{Domain}(R) = \{a \in A : (a, b) \in R\}$ collects the first entries and the range collects the second. Passing to $R^{-1}$ swaps domain and range.

nodes.label: Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
nodes.note: Reflexive demands $(a, a) \in R$ for all $a$, symmetric demands $aRb \Rightarrow bRa$, and transitive demands $aRb, bRc \Rightarrow aRc$. One missing pair destroys each property.

nodes.label: Example: Counting Reflexive Relations
nodes.note: On an $n$-element set the diagonal pairs are forced, so reflexive relations number $2^{n^2 - n}$. For $n = 3$ that is $2^6 = 64$ out of $2^9 = 512$ total relations.

nodes.label: Inverse and Composition
nodes.note: $R^{-1} = \{(b, a) : (a, b) \in R\}$ and $(S \circ R)^{-1} = R^{-1} \circ S^{-1}$. Composition is not commutative in general, so the order of the arrows matters.

nodes.label: Equivalence Relations
nodes.note: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive at once. Such relations split the set into clean, non-overlapping classes.

nodes.label: Definition of an Equivalence Relation
nodes.note: A relation that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Standard examples are equality, congruence modulo $n$ and 'born in the same year'.

nodes.label: Equivalence Classes
nodes.note: $[a] = \{x \in A : (x, a) \in R\}$, and any two classes are either identical or disjoint. The classes partition $A$, so their cardinalities add up to $n(A)$.

nodes.label: Example: Classes Modulo 3
nodes.note: Congruence mod 3 splits $\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}$ into the three classes $\{-2, 1\}$, $\{-1, 2\}$ and $\{0, 3\}$, which are disjoint and together cover the set.

nodes.label: Combining Equivalence Relations
nodes.note: If $R$ and $S$ are equivalence relations then $R \cap S$ is again an equivalence relation, but $R \cup S$ need not be. The inverse $R^{-1}$ of an equivalence relation is always one.
